title_original: Uncanny Valley: The OSTILLO Art Foundation
excerpt_original: A mysterious art foundation settles in among the driverless cars, software multinationals and property shell companies of a changing East Austin landscape. Jenny Wu thinks it might be right at home

blocks.text: A mysterious art foundation settles in among the driverless cars, software multinationals and property shell companies of a changing East Austin landscape. Jenny Wu thinks it might be right at home

In September, MASS Gallery held a 20th-anniversary party in its yard, at one end of which is a flat-roofed building housing its exhibition space. That evening, the space housed a selection of smallscale paintings, photographs and mixed-media works by past members of the LGBTQIA+ contemporary art organisation – the longest-running volunteer-based arts collective in Austin, Texas. I learned this from Erin Gentry, who’s been a member for 15 years. Other parts of the yard are occupied by Time Being Books, a bookstore run by archivist Addie Oscher, and Lynny’s, a food trailer owned by Gentry and her wife, Lynn.

blocks.caption: Exterior of OSTILLO, 2026. Courtesy the OSTILLO Art Foundation, Austin, Texas

blocks.text: Concurrently, a five-minute drive north, the grand opening of the OSTILLO Art Foundation was underway. This event featured the same basic setup: an outdoor gathering place, food trucks, an indoor art gallery, books (in the form of a public reference library). But the guests at OSTILLO were so dispersed across the foundation’s landscaped lawn – which is exponentially larger than MASS’s yard – that, seen from the second-floor balcony of the library in the back of the field, the artworld set looked like mirages trekking up the path in their wide-brimmed hats and leather boots. Other incongruities emerged.

‘Mysterious’ was the word Austin-based gallerists and journalists had used to describe OSTILLO. Many of them had learned of its existence via social media: an uncaptioned Instagram post from May reveals the facade of the building: a converted warehouse-type former daycare centre on the property of OSTILLO’s founder, René Campos, a real-estate developer whose company, Eureka Holdings, Inc, is reportedly the single largest landholder in the neighbourhood, having ‘quietly’ amassed an outsize portfolio of East Austin properties during the 2010s. The building, painted a uniform matt black, greeted us like a host without a face.

blocks.caption: Installation view of Masquerade at OSTILLO, 2026. Courtesy the OSTILLO Art Foundation, Austin, Texas

blocks.text: For its inaugural exhibition, the foundation mounted a group show titled Masquerade featuring an assortment of representative works by top-selling artists like Marlene Dumas, Sanya Kantarovsky, Glenn Ligon, Adam Pendleton, Mohammed Sami, Thomas Schütte, Salman Toor and Christopher Wool, coming primarily out of Campos’s private collection. Lacking an aesthetic bent or bias, the exhibition and, by extension, the collection gave the impression of a ghostless shell, not unlike the autonomous vehicles congesting the city’s roads (some have taken to calling Austin ‘Silicon Hills’ thanks to the arrival of Oracle and Tesla headquarters). The impersonality is exacerbated by the sparse install, whereby even largescale sculptures, like Schütte’s four bronze busts Fratelli (2012–20), and paintings, such as Sami’s pareidolia-inducing Religion Books (2004), look forsaken, eons away from their nearest neighbours.

The exhibition, which makes several nods to Rosewood, the historically Black neighbourhood in East Austin in which the foundation stands, hinges conceptually on Ligon’s Masquerade #9 (2006), a silkscreen near the entrance featuring the artist’s characteristically obscured text. According to the exhibition materials, the work quotes ‘Stranger in the Village’ (1953), an essay by American writer James Baldwin that reflects on summers he spent in the remote Swiss village of Leukerbad, where he encountered daily reminders of his otherness in the form of eerie images, like that of blue-eyed children donning horsehair wigs and blackface during carnaval .

blocks.caption: Installation view of Masquerade at OSTILLO, 2026. Courtesy the OSTILLO Art Foundation, Austin, Texas

blocks.text: The English word ‘uncanny’ – which is often translated to and from the German unheimlich, meaning, literally, ‘unhomelike’ – came to mind on OSTILLO’s overlarge lawn, and again in light of the rapid gentrification that Rosewood currently faces, which has displaced scores of longtime residents. A reminder that the place that was once home can gradually – or suddenly – cease to be so. The word reared its head again as I read local reports about the various legal monikers under which Eureka Holdings had purchased property in East Austin, ranging from 2015 Donut Wholes RC LP to 2017 Honk Honk LP. Other names include 2015 Beefy Gold Bullion LP, Poisonous Poinsettia LP and KB Swashbuckler 2007 LP. While not uncommon practice, this proliferation of identities caused certain lines from the exhibition press release – such as, ‘ Masquerade began with a very old human question: what do we choose to reveal, and what do we choose to conceal?’ – to read like clues in a familiar mystery.

Austin is small enough that most artists, gallerists and curators know each other. For instance, Gentry told me she has DJed at Ivester, a gallery where Austin-based artist Christine Garvey was showing mixed-media works exploring motherhood via nineteenth-century stage magic, whose owner Kevin Ivester, when I called him, was out with his young child visiting Martha’s, a gallery that was showing artist Hayley Labrum’s paintings, printed matter and ephemera related to Mormonism and her family. Over time, this art community may warm up to OSTILLO too. But it should also become apparent that their new neighbours are not new in town at all, that the foundation’s funder is no stranger to East Austin in the sense that Baldwin was to Leukerbad, but rather more like the villagers themselves – people who ‘cannot be, from the point of view of power,’ as Baldwin writes, ‘strangers anywhere in the world’.
